title-group.article-title: Robot‐Assisted Ileocecal Resection Using the Saroa Surgical System

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Saroa is a novel robotic surgical system that can estimate the gripping forces of robotic forceps and convey this information to the console surgeon via a remote‐control interface. A patient with a polyp located adjacent to the Bauhin valve was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma with submucosal and vascular invasion after endoscopic resection and subsequently underwent additional surgical resection. Port placement was modified twice intraoperatively due to the limited range of motion of the robotic arms. During the first setting, the ileocolic artery and vein were resected, and the ascending colon was mobilized. During the second setting, the hepatic flexure was mobilized. Further studies are needed to determine whether sensory feedback improves surgical safety and shortens the learning curve compared with other robotic platforms.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Robotic surgery may improve short‐term outcomes and oncological efficacy compared with laparoscopic surgery [1]. However, robot‐specific intraoperative complications, including accidental organ injury and mechanical malfunction, have been reported [2], highlighting the need to improve the robot–human interface, instrument robustness, and surgeon training.

Excessive force from robotic arms can cause tissue injury, a risk exacerbated by the lack of haptic feedback [3], which may partly explain limited improvement in surgical outcomes despite increased accuracy and dexterity [4]. Although robotic arms reduced pancreatic compression time during gastrectomy, a risk factor for leakage, complication rates did not decrease, and excessive instrument force was implicated [5].

Saroa (RIVERFIELD Inc., Tokyo, Japan) is a novel robotic surgical system available in Japan for gastrointestinal, urological, thoracic (excluding cardiovascular), and gynecological procedures. It provides grip‐force feedback, and brief training improves force‐controlled grasping [6], potentially enabling gentler tissue handling. Furthermore, Saroa has three arms and requires no port docking; however, its fewer arms relative to the da Vinci system necessitate close assistant cooperation. Although Saroa has been clinically applied in urologic and thoracic surgery, its use in gastrointestinal cancer remains limited. Herein, we report a case of ileocecal resection using Saroa.

sec.title: Case Presentation
sec.p: A man in his late 70s with a history of appendectomy presented with hematochezia. Colonoscopy identified multiple polyps, which were resected endoscopically. Histopathologic examination revealed submucosal and vascular invasion in a lesion adjacent to the Bauhin valve (0‐Ip, Tub1, submucosal invasion of 4000 μm, v1). The patient and his family were counseled regarding the risk of lymph node metastasis and offered two management options: additional surgical resection or surveillance. The patient elected robot‐assisted surgery. Preoperative contrast‐enhanced computed tomography showed no lymphadenopathy or distant metastases, and tumor marker levels were within normal limits. Ileocecal resection with D2 lymph node dissection was planned. Robotic surgery was performed following the 2024 Japanese Society for Cancer of the Colon and Rectum guidelines [7], relevant academic society guidelines, and institutional regulations. Under the general consent policy, the patient agreed to the anonymous use of clinical data for academic purposes.

sec.title: Port Placement Plan and Devices
sec.p: Saroa was used for robotic surgery. Optimal forceps manipulation was achieved within a 16 × 9 cm2 area extending approximately 9 cm anterior to the camera port (Figure S1). Therefore, the robotic setup was repositioned twice intraoperatively. Five ports were placed at the umbilicus and left upper, left lateral, left lower, and right lower abdomen (Figure S2). The left lateral abdominal port (initial camera port) was positioned approximately 4.5 cm lateral and slightly caudal to the umbilicus. The left upper, left lateral, and left lower abdominal ports were used to access the cecum and mid‐ascending colon (Figure 1A), whereas the right lower abdominal, umbilical, and left upper abdominal ports were used to access the hepatic flexure (Figure 1B). A 3D flexible scope with enabled sensory feedback and a 5:1 motion scale was used. Pneumoperitoneum was maintained using the AirSeal system with a 12‐mm access port (CONMED, Largo, FL) in the right lower abdomen. A Kii balloon blunt‐tip access system (Applied Medical, Rancho Santa Margarita, CA) was used at the umbilical port, and VersaOne 12‐mm trocars (Medtronic plc, Dublin, Ireland) were used at the remaining sites to facilitate smooth robotic arm movement.

caption.p: Port placement and setting. (A) Three ports in the left abdomen were initially used for the Saroa robot arms to manipulate blood vessels and mobilize the cecum and part of the ascending colon. The green and yellow circles indicate the optimal range for port insertion for each robot arm; ideally, port locations should fall within the green circle. (B) Ports at the left upper abdomen, umbilicus, and right lower abdomen were used for the Saroa robot arms. Red dots: 12 mm ports. L, left arm; R, right arm; S, scope.

sec.title: First Setting of Saroa Arms
sec.p: An assistant was positioned caudally to the patient's right side. The ileocolic artery (ICA) and vein (ICV) were retracted ventrally with fenestrated grasping forceps, and the mesentery was incised. Central serosal incision over the vessels exposed the anterior surface of the superior mesenteric vein and the ICV root (Figure 2A), which were clipped and divided. After exposure of the duodenum and anterior pancreatic surface, the ICA root was clipped and divided (Figure 2B).

caption.p: Resection of the ileocecal artery and vein. (A) Root of the ileocecal vein. The scissors behind the vein were in Saroa's right arm. (B) The root of the ileocecal artery is shown. ICA, ileocolic artery; ICV, ileocolic vein; SMV, superior mesenteric vein.

sec.p: Subsequently, the assistant applied ventral and outward traction to the peripheral ICA, while a second assistant retracted the central mesentery ventrally. The surgeon grasped the dorsal membrane to mobilize the ascending colon. During the lateral peritoneal incision, the first assistant introduced fenestrated forceps from the right lower abdomen to grasp and retract the adipose tissue of the ascending colon medially. The second assistant retracted the ileocolic folds from the umbilical port, while the left Saroa arm retracted the peritoneum laterally to the ascending colon.

sec.title: Second Setting of Saroa Arms
sec.p: To mobilize the hepatic flexure, the camera arm was inserted through the umbilical port, the right Saroa arm through the left upper abdominal port, and the left Saroa arm through the right lower abdominal port. To minimize instrument interference, the right arm was occasionally repositioned to the left lateral abdominal port. The assistant primarily retracted the colon toward the own port, while the surgeon's left hand provided lateral countertraction to facilitate incision and dissection. After mobilization, the colon containing the lesion was exteriorized through a mini‐laparotomy, resected, and reconstructed with a functional end‐to‐end anastomosis.

The total operative time was 351 min, including a console time of 182 min, with an estimated blood loss of 60 mL. The first bowel movement occurred on postoperative Day (POD) 5. However, paralytic ileus developed, as confirmed by physical examination and computed tomography. The ileus resolved with conservative management, oral intake resumed on POD 11, and the patient was discharged on POD 14. Pathologic examination demonstrated no residual tumor or lymph node metastasis among 11 retrieved lymph nodes.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The Saroa surgical system provides haptic (grip) feedback, enabling delicate tissue manipulation. A preclinical study evaluated whether sensory feedback improves material stiffness estimation and grip force regulation [6]. Although force feedback did not significantly improve stiffness estimation, brief training to calibrate a 3‐N grip force resulted in superior force control under feedback‐enabled conditions [6]. In the present case, the surgeon's extensive experience with other robotic platforms may explain the lack of apparent benefit of sensory feedback. However, with more cases, Saroa's haptic feedback may reduce the risk of mesenteric injury from excessive grasping force and help shorten the learning curve for less experienced robotic surgeons.

Because Saroa is limited to three arms, the assistant plays a critical role. In contrast, da Vinci systems utilize a fourth arm (e.g., a Tip‐Up Fenestrated Grasper) for operative field stabilization. Therefore, with Saroa, effective assistant traction and close surgeon‐assistant coordination are essential. In addition to technical skill and anatomical knowledge, surgeons must account for the limited range of motion of assistant forceps and potential collisions with robotic arms. Thus, future improvements may include optimized port placement, addition of a robotic arm, or effective use of an internal organ retractor [8]. Another limitation is the narrow workspace in which the Saroa arms can operate smoothly, necessitating two robotic setups (Figure 1). Despite this adjustment, hepatic flexure mobilization remained challenging. Laparoscopic observation was required in the final phase to confirm organ integrity, and additional incisions were selectively made where mobilization was insufficient. A hybrid approach combining robotic precision for vascular manipulation with laparoscopic mobilization may shorten operative time.

Through this surgery, several areas requiring improvement in the Saroa system were identified. Saroa adopts a nondocking mechanism between ports and arms, similar to the Hinotori system (Medicaroid Co., Kobe, Hyogo, Japan) [9], which may cause port‐arm friction and intermittent motion, warranting further refinement. Limited availability of energy devices necessitates precise dissection with an electric scalpel, potentially prolonging surgical time and hemostasis. Furthermore, Saroa lacks traction force and shaft compression feedback, features available in the da Vinci 5 system (Intuitive Surgical, Sunnyvale, CA) [10], representing important targets for future development.

Saroa is relatively affordable and lightweight, often eliminating the need for operating room reinforcement for load‐bearing capacity. Although exact costs are undetermined, running costs are estimated to be lower than those of other systems. These factors are particularly important in Japan, where sustaining robotic surgery is economically challenging under the current reimbursement structure [11]. Comparative studies evaluating economic burden are warranted, considering operative time, postoperative complications, and the requirement of experienced assistance. Given the potential advantages, we expect that the use of Saloa will be expanded to other colorectal cancer surgeries, beyond sigmoidectomy [12] and ileocecal resection, and benign conditions such as rectal prolapse upon addressing the listed issuers.

In conclusion, we report a case of ileocolic resection using the Saroa surgical system. Further studies are needed to determine whether sensory feedback improves procedural safety and shortens the learning curve.
